concepts.title: Async and Concurrency
concepts.description: Concurrency and parallelism are different things; the GIL means threads don't give standard Python true CPU parallelism; and async/await runs on a single-threaded event loop that helps with I/O-bound waiting but does nothing for CPU-bound work.
learningObjectives: Distinguish concurrency (interleaving many tasks) from parallelism (running tasks literally at the same time).
Explain what the GIL is and why it prevents true CPU parallelism between threads in standard Python.
Choose between threads, processes, and asyncio based on whether a workload is I/O-bound or CPU-bound.
Explain async/await and the event loop's cooperative scheduling model without treating it as automatic parallelism.
Predict why converting a CPU-bound function to async provides no speedup, and identify what would actually help.

sections.heading: Concurrency vs. Parallelism
sections.body:
People use these two words interchangeably, but they mean different things. **Concurrency** means making progress on multiple tasks over the same span of time, by interleaving them: working a bit on task A, switching to task B while A is stuck waiting on something, coming back to A once it's ready, and so on. It doesn't require two things to happen at the same instant, only that no time is wasted while one task is idle. **Parallelism** means multiple tasks are physically executing at the same moment, typically on different CPU cores.

Compare a single chef cooking three dishes by starting the rice, then while it simmers chopping vegetables for the second dish, then while those saute checking on a sauce for the third: that's concurrency. One chef, never doing two things in the same instant, still finishes sooner than cooking each dish start to finish. Three separate chefs, each with their own stove, cooking three dishes at the same time: that's parallelism. A program can be concurrent without being parallel, which is why asyncio helps with some problems and not others.

sections.heading: The GIL: Why Threads Don't Give You True CPU Parallelism
sections.body:
Standard Python (CPython, the reference implementation almost everyone uses) has a **Global Interpreter Lock** (GIL): a single lock that only one thread can hold at a time, and holding it is required to execute Python bytecode. So even if your program creates ten threads, only *one* of them is ever executing Python code at any given instant; the others are waiting their turn for the GIL, no matter how many CPU cores your machine has. The GIL exists mainly for implementation simplicity and safety: it protects CPython's internal memory management (reference counting for garbage collection) from race conditions without needing much finer-grained, and much more complex, locking throughout the interpreter.

The practical consequence: for CPU-bound work (code that's crunching numbers, transforming data, running tight loops) Python threads do **not** give you a speedup from using multiple cores, because the GIL ensures only one thread's Python bytecode runs at a time regardless of core count. Adding threads to a CPU-bound task only adds the overhead of passing the lock between them, which can make things *slower*.

Two qualifications. Other implementations (Jython, for example) have no GIL, and CPython itself now has a separate **free-threaded build** without one: experimental in 3.13, officially supported but still optional in 3.14. The ordinary `python` you install still has the GIL. And C extensions can release it: NumPy and `zlib`, for instance, drop the lock during long operations, so threads can use several cores there.

sections.heading: Threads vs. Processes vs. asyncio
sections.body:
Given the GIL, Python offers three concurrency tools, and picking one starts with a question: **is the workload spending most of its time waiting on something external (I/O-bound), or spending most of its time actively computing (CPU-bound)?**

- **Threads** (`threading`): multiple threads within a single process, sharing memory. Because of the GIL, threads don't help CPU-bound work, but they *do* help I/O-bound work: when a thread is blocked waiting on a network response, a disk read, or similar, it releases the GIL while waiting, letting another thread run Python code in the meantime. Good fit: I/O-bound tasks where you want or need blocking-style, traditional synchronous-looking code (e.g. using a library that isn't async-aware) run concurrently.
- **Processes** (`multiprocessing`): multiple separate OS processes, each with its own Python interpreter and its own GIL, meaning they can run on separate CPU cores at the same moment. This is the tool that achieves parallelism for CPU-bound work, at the cost of more overhead (starting a process is heavier than starting a thread) and no shared memory by default (data has to be serialized and passed between processes, which has its own cost). Good fit: CPU-bound work like heavy numeric computation, image or video processing, or anything limited by how fast the CPU can crunch through data.
- **asyncio**: a single thread, running a single event loop, that cooperatively switches between many tasks whenever one of them is waiting on I/O. No threads, no processes, no GIL contention between multiple Python-executing threads at all: just one thread, doing one thing at a time, but very efficiently avoiding ever sitting idle while something else could be making progress. Good fit: a very large number of concurrent I/O-bound operations (thousands of open network connections, for instance), where the overhead of one OS thread per task would be prohibitive, and where the libraries involved are async-aware.

Reach for the wrong one (threads or asyncio for CPU-bound work) and you get sequential speed plus extra complexity.

sections.heading: async/await and the Event Loop
sections.body:
`async def` defines a **coroutine function**. Calling it doesn't run its body immediately; it returns a coroutine object that has to be driven by something else (the event loop) to execute. `await` marks a point where a coroutine can pause and hand control back to the event loop, at a spot where it's waiting on something (typically I/O) rather than doing active computation:

```python
import asyncio

async def fetch_page(name, delay):
    print(f"Starting {name}")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)   # simulates waiting on a network response
    print(f"Finished {name}")
    return f"{name} result"

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch_page("A", 2),
        fetch_page("B", 1),
    )
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
```

The event loop is a single-threaded loop that keeps track of tasks and repeatedly runs whichever are ready to make progress. When `fetch_page("A", 2)` hits `await asyncio.sleep(2)`, it doesn't block the whole program for two seconds. It tells the event loop "I have nothing more to do until this two-second timer finishes; go run something else in the meantime." The event loop then switches to `fetch_page("B", 1)`, runs it until *it* hits an await point, and keeps going between whichever tasks are ready. So the output prints "Starting A", "Starting B" nearly immediately (both begin, then both immediately hit their await and yield control), then "Finished B" around the 1-second mark, then "Finished A" around the 2-second mark, totaling roughly 2 seconds overall, not 3, which is what running them one after another sequentially would have taken. Nothing here runs in parallel; one thread does one thing at a time, but never sits idle while something is ready.

Because scheduling is cooperative, a blocking call breaks it: `time.sleep(2)` or `requests.get(...)` inside a coroutine freezes every other task until it returns. If you have to use a blocking library, `await asyncio.to_thread(func, ...)` moves the call to a worker thread.

sections.heading: Why Making a CPU-Bound Function async Doesn't Help
sections.body:
After asyncio speeds up some network-heavy code, people often try the same on a slow, CPU-heavy function. It doesn't work. The event loop's trick is *switching to other work while a task is waiting on something external*. A CPU-bound function (one that's actively computing the whole time, with no I/O to wait on) never hits an `await` point where it's idle; it just runs, using the CPU, from start to finish. Marking it `async def` and awaiting it doesn't change that at all: the event loop hands it control, it runs to completion doing pure computation with the GIL held throughout, and *only then* does it return control to the loop. Nothing else gets a chance to run during that stretch. You've achieved zero overlap, because there was never any idle waiting time to overlap with in the first place. Worse, if this happens inside an app that's also handling other async tasks (like serving other users' requests), that long CPU-bound stretch blocks *everything else* in the event loop too: one 500 ms computation adds 500 ms to every request being served at that moment.

The fix is to reach for the tool that matches the workload: run CPU-bound work in a separate process (`multiprocessing`, or `asyncio`'s own `loop.run_in_executor()` combined with a `ProcessPoolExecutor`, which runs the work in another process and gives you something to `await` in the meantime).

examples.title: Overlapping Many Network Requests
examples.code:
import asyncio
import time

async def fetch(name, seconds):
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)   # stands in for a network call
    return f"{name} done"

async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("request-1", 1),
        fetch("request-2", 1),
        fetch("request-3", 1),
    )
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(results)
    print(f"Took {elapsed:.1f}s")   # ~1.0s, not ~3.0s

asyncio.run(main())
examples.explanation: Each fetch() call simulates a network request that takes 1 second, spent waiting rather than computing. asyncio.gather() starts all three coroutines and lets the event loop run them concurrently: when the first hits await asyncio.sleep(1), it yields control back to the loop instead of blocking the whole program, letting the second and third start their own waits almost immediately afterward. Because all three are waiting on independent one-second timers at roughly the same time, the total elapsed time is close to 1 second, not 3: the waiting overlapped rather than stacking up sequentially. The same holds for hundreds or thousands of HTTP requests on a single thread. In practice you'd cap the number in flight (with an `asyncio.Semaphore`, for example) so you don't overload the server you're calling.

examples.title: asyncio Doing Nothing for CPU-Bound Work
examples.code:
import asyncio
import time

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
    return True

async def count_primes_async(start, end):
    # marking this 'async' changes nothing about how it executes --
    # there is no await anywhere inside it, because there's nothing to wait on
    return sum(1 for n in range(start, end) if is_prime(n))

async def main():
    start_time = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        count_primes_async(0, 200_000),
        count_primes_async(200_000, 400_000),
    )
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start_time
    print(results)
    print(f"Took {elapsed:.2f}s")   # roughly the same as running both sequentially, back to back

asyncio.run(main())
examples.explanation: count_primes_async is declared async def, and it's awaited via asyncio.gather() like the network example above, but there is no await anywhere inside its body, because checking whether numbers are prime is pure CPU computation with nothing to wait on. When the event loop runs the first call, it executes start to finish without ever yielding control back, because it never hits a point where it has nothing to do but wait. It always has more computing to do, right up until it returns a result. The second call then has to wait for the first call to finish before it even gets a turn, since the loop is single-threaded and the first call never released control. The total time ends up roughly equal to running both ranges one after another sequentially. Speeding this up means running the two ranges in separate OS processes (e.g. via concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor), so they can execute on separate CPU cores at the same time, which asyncio alone never does.

misconceptions.description: If I make my slow, CPU-heavy function async and await it, it'll run faster, the same way asyncio sped up my network request code.
misconceptions.clarification: asyncio's speedup comes from filling otherwise-idle waiting time with other useful work: when a coroutine hits await on something that's waiting (a network response, a timer), the event loop switches to another task instead of sitting idle. A CPU-bound function has no idle waiting time at all; it's actively using the CPU from the moment it starts until the moment it finishes. Wrapping it in async def and awaiting it doesn't create any waiting time that wasn't there before. The function still runs start to finish as one uninterrupted block, and while it runs, nothing else in the event loop gets a turn either, since everything shares that one thread. The fix for a CPU-bound bottleneck is a separate process (true parallelism across CPU cores), not asyncio, which only ever helps with I/O-bound waiting.

misconceptions.description: Python threads don't give real parallelism for CPU-bound work, so there's no point ever using threading in Python -- just use asyncio or multiprocessing for everything.
misconceptions.clarification: Threads remain useful for I/O-bound work, because a thread that's blocked waiting on I/O (a network call, a file read, many blocking library calls) releases the GIL while it waits, letting other threads run Python code during that idle time. Threads are also often the simplest option when you need to run traditional, blocking-style code concurrently (for instance, using a library with no async API) without rewriting everything around an event loop. The narrower rule is: don't expect threads to speed up CPU-bound Python code.

exercises.prompt: What is printed, and in roughly what order, and about how long does main() take to run in total?
exercises.code:
import asyncio

async def worker(name, delay):
    print(f"{name} starting")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"{name} finished")

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(
        worker("A", 3),
        worker("B", 1),
    )

asyncio.run(main())
hints: Both worker() calls start running almost immediately when gather() launches them. Neither has to wait for the other to finish before it even begins.
Each worker prints its 'starting' message, then immediately hits await asyncio.sleep(...) and yields control back to the event loop. It doesn't block anything else while it waits.
The two sleeps run concurrently, not back-to-back, the total time is determined by whichever delay is longest, not by adding the delays together.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'A starting' and 'B starting' print first, in that order (roughly together, since both begin almost immediately), then 'B finished' after about 1 second, then 'A finished' after about 3 seconds total. The whole thing takes roughly 3 seconds overall, not 4, because the two sleeps overlap concurrently rather than running one after the other.
exercises.solutionExplanation: asyncio.gather() starts both worker() coroutines essentially together. Each one prints its 'starting' message first, then immediately hits await asyncio.sleep(delay), handing control back to the event loop rather than blocking. Since both are now just waiting on independent timers, the event loop has nothing else to run, and the two timers count down together. B's 1-second timer finishes first, printing 'B finished' around the 1-second mark, and A's 3-second timer finishes later, printing 'A finished' around the 3-second mark. Total elapsed time for main() is roughly 3 seconds, governed by the longer of the two delays, rather than 4 seconds, which is what running them one after the other would have taken.

exercises.prompt: You've written an async web scraper that fetches many pages concurrently using aiohttp-style async requests, and it works great -- fast, efficient, handles hundreds of pages without spawning hundreds of threads. Now a teammate adds a step that runs after each page is fetched: a CPU-heavy text analysis function (parsing and scoring the page's text, taking about 200ms of pure computation per page) that has no I/O in it at all. They wrote it as `async def analyze(text): ...` with no `await` inside, and awaited it alongside the fetches, expecting it to stay fast. Explain what will actually happen to overall throughput, and rewrite the analysis step so it doesn't stall the rest of the scraper's concurrency.
hints: Ask whether analyze() ever yields control back to the event loop. Does it contain any await pointing at something waiting on I/O?

Because analyze() is pure computation with no await inside, once the event loop starts running it, nothing else (including other pages' fetches that are ready to proceed) gets a turn until it fully finishes.

Look for a way to hand CPU-bound work off to something other than the event loop's single thread, while still being able to await its eventual result from within async code. concurrent.futures has a tool for this, paired with an event loop's executor support.
exercises.solutionCode:
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

async def fetch_page(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)          # stand-in for the real aiohttp request
    return f"text of {url}"

def analyze_sync(text):
    # stand-in for the real CPU-heavy analysis, as an ordinary (non-async) function
    return sum(len(word) for word in text.split())

async def analyze(text, executor):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    # runs analyze_sync in a separate process, and awaits the result
    # without blocking the event loop's single thread while it runs
    return await loop.run_in_executor(executor, analyze_sync, text)

async def process_page(url, executor):
    text = await fetch_page(url)           # I/O-bound: overlaps with other fetches
    score = await analyze(text, executor)  # CPU-bound: runs in another process
    return score

async def main(urls):
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:
        return await asyncio.gather(*(process_page(url, executor) for url in urls))

if __name__ == "__main__":   # required: worker processes may re-import this file
    print(asyncio.run(main(["/a", "/b", "/c"])))   # [8, 8, 8]
exercises.solutionExplanation: Declaring analyze() as async def with no await inside it doesn't change how it executes at all. It still runs as one uninterrupted, 200ms block of pure computation, and during that stretch, the single-threaded event loop cannot switch to anything else, including other pages' fetches that may already be sitting ready to proceed. With hundreds of pages, those 200ms blocks pile up serially on the one thread, one after another, which cancels the concurrency the scraper was built to get. The fix hands the CPU-heavy work off to a ProcessPoolExecutor (a pool of separate OS processes) via loop.run_in_executor(), which schedules analyze_sync to run in another process (in parallel with the main event loop and with other worker processes, since each process has its own GIL) and returns an awaitable that the event loop CAN treat as a waiting point, freeing it to keep servicing other pages' fetches while the analysis runs elsewhere. The I/O-bound fetch step stays as it was, since asyncio already handles that well; only the CPU-bound step needed a different tool. The if __name__ == "__main__" guard matters here: with the spawn and forkserver start methods (spawn is the default on Windows and macOS), each worker process re-imports the script, and without the guard it would try to start the pool again.

assessments.prompt: A Python program spawns four threads, each running a tight numeric loop that does heavy computation with no I/O at all, on a machine with four free CPU cores. What should you expect?
options: A speedup proportional to the number of cores, but only for numeric code specifically, since numeric operations are exempt from the GIL.
No meaningful speedup over running the same work in a single thread.
The program will raise a runtime error, since CPython does not allow multiple threads to run CPU-bound code at all.
Roughly a 4x speedup, since there are four threads and four free cores available.
assessments.explanation: The GIL ensures that only one thread executes Python bytecode at any given instant, no matter how many CPU cores are idle and available. So four threads doing CPU-bound work don't run four-way in parallel; they take turns on a single core's worth of execution, with some added overhead from switching the GIL between them. The “Roughly a 4x speedup, since there…” option describes what would happen with true parallelism (e.g. via separate processes), which threading does not provide for CPU-bound work in CPython. The “The program will raise a runtime error…” option is wrong. This code runs fine, just without the parallel speedup someone might expect. The “A speedup proportional to the number…” option is a fabricated exemption; there is no general carve-out for numeric code (certain C-extension libraries can release the GIL internally during specific operations, but that's a property of those specific libraries' implementation, not a blanket rule about 'numeric code').

assessments.prompt: You're building a tool that needs to do two things: (1) download and process metadata for 5,000 URLs from a remote API, and (2) run a computationally expensive image-resizing operation on 500 local image files. Explain which concurrency approach -- threading, multiprocessing, or asyncio -- fits each part best, and why using the same tool for both parts would be a mistake.
assessments.modelAnswer: The two parts have different bottlenecks. Downloading metadata for 5,000 URLs is I/O-bound (almost all the time is spent waiting on network responses, not computing anything), which is the shape of problem asyncio is built for: a single thread can have thousands of requests in flight at once, switching to whichever one is ready to make progress whenever another is stuck waiting on the network, with far less overhead than spinning up 5,000 OS threads. Resizing 500 images, on the other hand, is CPU-bound. The bottleneck is how fast the CPU can crunch through pixel data, with little to no waiting involved. asyncio would provide no benefit here at all, since there's no idle waiting time for an event loop to fill with other work; each resize would just run start to finish as one uninterrupted block, as if it were called. Pure-Python resizing code wouldn't gain from threading either, since the GIL means only one thread's Python bytecode runs at a time, so four threads each resizing images wouldn't run four resizes in parallel. They'd take turns. (Some imaging libraries release the GIL inside their C code, and then threads can help; measure before choosing.) multiprocessing is the right tool for this half: spreading the 500 images across several separate OS processes, each with its own GIL, lets multiple images be resized at the same time on separate CPU cores. Using asyncio for the image resizing would leave that part just as slow as doing it sequentially (while adding unnecessary complexity), and using multiprocessing for 5,000 network requests would work but waste a large amount of memory and process-startup overhead for a problem that a single async event loop could handle far more efficiently. Picking the tool that matches each workload's bottleneck matters more than picking one tool and forcing both problems through it.

assessments.prompt: A single-core machine runs a program using asyncio to handle 100 concurrent network requests. Is this concurrency, parallelism, both, or neither?
options: Concurrency only -- the requests are interleaved on a single thread while waiting on I/O, but nothing is literally executing at the same physical instant, which is what parallelism would require
Parallelism only, since 100 requests are genuinely all 'in flight' at once
Both concurrency and parallelism, since asyncio's event loop always uses multiple CPU cores internally to manage its scheduling
Neither -- true concurrency requires at least two physical CPU cores to begin with
assessments.explanation: Concurrency is about structure (making progress on multiple tasks by interleaving them, never wasting time while one is idle) and requires nothing about the underlying hardware. Parallelism requires multiple things physically happening at the same literal instant, which a single core can never provide, since it runs one thread of execution at a time. asyncio's event loop is concurrency without parallelism: many tasks make progress over the same span of time by interleaving whenever one is waiting, but at any given instant, only one is executing.

assessments.prompt: What is the primary reason CPython's GIL exists?
options: It's a requirement imposed by Python's open-source license terms
To make Python code run faster on multi-core machines by automatically coordinating work across cores
To prevent programmers from accidentally writing infinite loops in threaded code
To protect CPython's internal memory management (reference counting for garbage collection) from race conditions, without requiring much more complex, fine-grained locking throughout the interpreter
assessments.explanation: The GIL exists mainly for implementation simplicity and safety: it protects CPython's internal reference-counting garbage collector from race conditions using one single, simple lock, rather than requiring much finer-grained locking scattered throughout the interpreter's internals. It has nothing to do with license terms (“It's a requirement imposed by Python's open-source license terms”), doesn't prevent infinite loops (“To prevent programmers from accidentally writing infinite…”), and works against multi-core speedups for CPU-bound code rather than coordinating or enabling them (the “To make Python code run faster…” option is backwards).

assessments.prompt: A program creates 10 threads, each making a blocking network request expected to take about 2 seconds, all starting at roughly the same time. Approximately how long should the whole batch take, and why?
options: About 20 seconds total, since the GIL forces the threads to run strictly one at a time even while they're blocked waiting on I/O
About 2 seconds, but only because the GIL is entirely disabled for the whole program the moment any network operation begins
About 2 seconds total -- each thread releases the GIL while blocked waiting on its network response
It depends entirely on the number of CPU cores available, since each thread needs its own dedicated core to make any progress at all
assessments.explanation: Threads help here despite the GIL: a thread blocked on I/O (waiting for a network response) releases the GIL for the duration of that wait, letting other threads run Python code (or start their own blocking calls) while it waits. Since all 10 requests are waiting on their own independent ~2-second network responses at roughly the same time, that waiting overlaps, and the whole batch finishes in roughly 2 seconds, not 20. This doesn't require multiple CPU cores (“It depends entirely on the number…”). Releasing the GIL during I/O wait is what makes the overlap possible, not simultaneous execution on separate cores.

assessments.prompt: Which of these is a genuine cost or tradeoff of using multiprocessing instead of threading, according to this lesson?
options: Processes are fundamentally unable to run on more than one CPU core at the same time, unlike threads
multiprocessing is not part of the Python standard library and must be installed separately
Starting a new process carries more overhead than starting a new thread
Processes all share the exact same GIL, so there's no actual benefit over threading for CPU-bound work
assessments.explanation: Each process gets its own separate Python interpreter and its own GIL, and starting one is heavier than starting a thread, plus there's no shared memory by default. Any data that needs to move between processes has to be serialized and passed across, which costs time. That is the tradeoff multiprocessing accepts in exchange for true CPU parallelism. The “Processes are fundamentally unable to run…” and “Processes all share the exact same GIL…” options describe the opposite of what happens (multiple GILs, one per process, is what enables parallelism), and multiprocessing is a standard library module, not a third-party dependency (“multiprocessing is not part of the Python…”).

assessments.prompt:
```python
import asyncio

async def worker(name, delay):
    print(f"{name} start")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"{name} end")

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(worker("X", 2), worker("Y", 2), worker("Z", 1))

asyncio.run(main())
```
What's the order of printed output, and roughly how long does main() take?
options: X start / Y start / Z start / Z end / X end / Y end -- total time about 5 seconds
X start / Y start / Z start / Z end / X end / Y end -- total time about 2 seconds
Z start / Z end / X start / X end / Y start / Y end -- total time about 5 seconds
X start / Y start / Z start / X end / Y end / Z end -- total time about 5 seconds
assessments.explanation: asyncio.gather() starts all three coroutines together; each prints its 'start' message and immediately hits await asyncio.sleep(...), yielding control back to the event loop. All three sleeps then run concurrently rather than sequentially: Z's 1-second timer finishes first, printing 'Z end' around the 1-second mark, and X's and Y's 2-second timers finish together afterward, around the 2-second mark, in the order they were scheduled. The whole thing takes roughly 2 seconds total, governed by the *longest* delay among concurrently-running tasks, not the sum of all three delays (which would be 5 seconds if they ran one after another sequentially).

assessments.prompt:
```python
import asyncio

async def greet():
    print("hello")

coro = greet()
print("created")
```
What gets printed, in order?
options: created (only) -- calling greet() returns a coroutine object without running any of its body
hello then created
created then hello
It raises an error immediately, since a coroutine object can't be created without an event loop already running
assessments.explanation: Calling an async def function does not execute its body. Just like calling a generator function, it immediately returns an object (here, a coroutine object) that has to be driven by something else, the event loop, in order to run. Since coro is never awaited, passed to asyncio.run(), or scheduled in any other way, the body of greet(), and therefore "hello", never executes in this snippet. "created" prints normally. When the never-awaited object is destroyed, Python also writes a warning to stderr: RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'greet' was never awaited. Creating a coroutine object doesn't require an event loop to already be running; only driving it to completion does.

assessments.prompt: According to this lesson, what is the correct fix for a genuinely CPU-bound function that's currently slowing down an otherwise-fast asyncio application?
options: Increase the number of internal threads the asyncio event loop itself uses
Just await the function directly -- async def functions are automatically scheduled onto a separate CPU core by the interpreter
Add extra await statements inside the CPU-bound function, even where there's nothing to actually wait on, so the event loop can interleave it more often
Run the CPU-bound work in a separate process (e.g. via multiprocessing, or loop.run_in_executor with a ProcessPoolExecutor)
assessments.explanation: Since the whole problem is that CPU-bound work has no idle waiting time for the event loop to fill with other tasks, the fix has to come from outside the event loop: running the work in a separate OS process gives it a separate GIL and, potentially, a separate CPU core, so it runs in parallel with the loop. Adding fake await points (“Add extra await statements inside the CPU-bound…”) creates no idle time to exploit: something like await asyncio.sleep(0) would let other tasks run between chunks, but the computation would still occupy the one thread and finish no sooner. The event loop is fundamentally single-threaded by design (the “Increase the number of internal threads…” option misunderstands this), and async def alone never causes automatic multi-core scheduling (“Just await the function directly -- async…”). A coroutine runs on the event loop's own thread.

assessments.prompt: Can a program achieve genuine parallelism on a machine with only one CPU core?
options: Yes, as long as the program creates enough threads
No -- parallelism specifically requires multiple execution units (such as multiple cores) doing work at the exact same instant
Yes, but only specifically for I/O-bound workloads
Yes, as long as the program uses asyncio's event loop, since the event loop itself runs in parallel with the tasks it schedules
assessments.explanation: Parallelism is fundamentally a hardware property: it requires more than one execution unit doing work at the same literal moment. A single CPU core (leaving aside hardware multithreading) runs one thread of execution at a time, however many threads or coroutines the program creates. More threads mean more things taking turns, which is concurrency, not parallelism. Neither threading (“Yes, as long as the program creates enough threads”) nor asyncio (“Yes, as long as the program uses…”) creates additional cores out of nothing, and this limitation is about the underlying hardware, not about whether the workload happens to be I/O-bound or CPU-bound (“Yes, but only specifically for I/O-bound workloads”).

assessments.prompt: A service needs to maintain roughly 10,000 simultaneous open network connections, each mostly idle, occasionally receiving a message. Which approach does this lesson describe as the best fit, and why?
options: None of Python's concurrency tools can realistically handle more than a few hundred simultaneous connections
threading -- one dedicated thread per connection is always the simplest and most efficient choice, at any scale
multiprocessing -- one process per connection ensures each connection gets genuine, dedicated CPU parallelism
asyncio -- a single thread can efficiently track thousands of waiting tasks, whereas dedicating one OS thread to each connection would carry prohibitive overhead at that scale
assessments.explanation: This is where asyncio fits best: a very large number of concurrent, mostly-idle I/O-bound operations, where the overhead of one OS thread (or, far worse, one OS process) per connection would be prohibitive at scale. A single event loop can track thousands of waiting connections efficiently, switching to whichever one has a message ready, without needing anywhere near 10,000 separate OS-level threads or processes, each of which carries memory and scheduling overhead that makes the “threading -- one dedicated thread per connection…” and “multiprocessing -- one process per connection ensures…” options impractical at this scale.
